# Milestone 7 evidence

The complete acceptance command passed at source `ab3f2a1102db132ab60ec26afd69a7784b1e1c67`.

```sh
env -u DISPLAY python3 tools/verify.py --sanitize --presentation --isolated-display
```

The [acceptance record](m7-acceptance.json) identifies the source, exit status, component outcomes and artifact hashes. The [complete log](m7-verification.log) preserves the actual command progression. The [native capture](m7-native-atelier.png) shows the tested default Atelier window.

## Correctness

- Exact geometry checks include independent original Body state, pinned cuts, dirty boundaries, canonical order and byte-identical output with one and six workers. A coherent material mutation fails the negative control.
- Actual device checks cover reusable staging, atomic whole-set retirement, failed-publication rollback, recorded references, two pending submissions and independent readbacks.
- Acquisition checks cover every byte of the 2,336-byte appearance input, distinct camera and shadow data, submission order independent of body revision, reversed completion observation and obsolete-lease cleanup.
- Native windows pass with shared and distinct queue pairs 0/0 and 0/2. Checks include edits, reset, flight, resize, suspension, remap, close and ordinary quiet launch. Traced shutdown checks reach zero rows.
- Khronos and synchronization validation and actual ASan/UBSan execution pass on NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 under Linux/X11.

The [195 archived/current offscreen RGBA comparisons](m7-appearance-diff.json) contain 171 exact captures. The remaining 24 shaded captures differ by at most four channel units. Exact geometry, identity and current shadow-causality gates pass. Shaded output is not byte-identical to the old implementation. The native old/new measurement driver retains a stricter exact static RGB eligibility rule. The [production manifest](m7-production-source-manifest.json) preserves source and capture hashes from the passing full run.

## Performance

The overall production-performance verdict is inconclusive. The [old/new comparison](m7-old-new.json) has no eligible timing pairs. All 20 native processes exited zero and all 160 edit actions completed, including warmup. All ten timing pairs were excluded by exact static RGB mismatches. No implementation speedup is established.

The independent [instrumented profile](m7-profile.json) passed four runs. Whole-run application CPU averages range from 2.18 to 2.55 cores, and the sampled observer process averages range from 0.08 to 0.10 cores. Producer record/submit medians are about 20.5 ms. The two flight runs have main-pass inclusive GPU medians of 0.601 and 0.624 ms. The two edit runs have main-pass medians of 1.431 and 1.441 ms. Upload and shadow medians are below 1 ms in all four runs. These observations point toward host recording and submission cost. They do not isolate individual renderer costs or account for every observer subprocess.

The profile includes polling, warmup and settling. CPU producer scopes can realize deferred Bend work. GPU TOP-to-BOTTOM windows can overlap and include preceding work. Device-wide GPU utilization includes the desktop. No call stacks or instrumentation-overhead estimate are available. Profile samples are excluded from comparative timings.

Flight comparisons share scripted input duration. Time-driven camera poses can differ, so they do not establish identical per-frame GPU work. Throughput counts observed matching presentation-resource fences, which permit resource reuse and may precede completion of presentation. Physical scanout is unmeasured. Edit latency includes event dispatch through observation of a completed frame tagged with the requested revision. Trace receipt, polling and scheduling delay remain included.

The [build record](m7-builds.json) identifies both ordinary executables, compiler evidence and source revisions. A [diagnostic of the first old/new pair](m7-native-image-diff.json) independently finds four changed RGB pixels in each static image, with a maximum channel difference of four. The [complete static-image report](m7-native-static-parity.json) records the same result for all 90 capture pairs. Geometry and view signatures match. These diagnostics change no eligibility rule and establish no cause for the difference.

The [CPU comparison](m7-cpu-1-6.json) holds the executable and one frame slot fixed. All 20 processes exit zero, all 160 edit actions complete and all output assertions pass. Each workload has five eligible alternating pairs. The table gives the median and range across runs. Cut and reset entries summarize each run's median of six measured actions; warmup actions are excluded from those timings.

| Observed metric | One worker | Six workers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Presentation-resource handoffs per second | 42.44, range 42.36 to 42.86 | 41.32, range 41.05 to 43.16 |
| Cut latency in ms | 1,207.5, range 1,202.0 to 1,231.4 | 1,669.2, range 1,645.3 to 1,682.5 |
| Reset latency in ms | 9,483.1, range 9,373.3 to 9,537.9 | 4,034.1, range 3,998.1 to 4,044.3 |

Flight ranges overlap. One worker has lower observed cut latency, while six workers have lower reset latency. This is a tradeoff for the traced configuration. It establishes no universal worker winner, implementation speedup or isolated CPU meshing speedup. The separate profile covers six workers and two slots, so it cannot establish the exact limiter for every CPU configuration. Trace overhead remains unmeasured. No production default changes follow from this sweep.

The [slot comparison](m7-slots-1-2.json) holds the executable and six workers fixed. All 20 processes exit zero, all 160 edit actions complete and all output assertions pass. Each workload has five eligible alternating pairs. The table uses the same per-run summary policy as the CPU comparison.

| Observed metric | One slot | Two slots |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Presentation-resource handoffs per second | 41.80, range 41.48 to 42.13 | 43.81, range 43.20 to 44.39 |
| Cut latency in ms | 1,666.1, range 1,638.9 to 1,681.8 | 1,687.5, range 1,667.5 to 1,716.6 |
| Reset latency in ms | 4,010.4, range 3,980.5 to 4,094.7 | 4,064.8, range 4,000.1 to 4,128.2 |

Two slots have a higher observed handoff rate in these traced flight runs. Cut and reset ranges overlap. The profile points toward host recording and submission cost, which limits the benefit available from GPU overlap. Dynamic flight poses differ and instrumentation overhead is unmeasured. The result supports the tested traced configuration and establishes no general production, physical display FPS or identical-work renderer speedup. The existing two-slot feature default remains. No different worker count was selected, so no slot sweep at another worker count was required.

Observed resource assertions pass in both configuration sweeps. Reset row ranges and half-window maxima stay within the driver's checks, and traced shutdown reaches zero rows. Native metadata allocation counters are absent at those checkpoints. These observations do not bound all heap or driver allocations and GPU bytes. Optional culling, allocation pooling and extra draw batching remain deferred. The available profile does not isolate their cost or establish a representative benefit.

import argparse
import os
from pathlib import Path
import re
import signal
import subprocess
import time

from check_window import X11, states, isolated_display, build_window, BUILD, ROOT

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=1800


def run(binary, split):
    suffix='split' if split else 'shared'
    path=BUILD/f'milestone-6-atelier-window-{suffix}.log'
    x=X11()
    env=dict(os.environ,VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS='VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation',VK_LAYER_VALIDATE_SYNC='1',
             ASAN_OPTIONS='detect_leaks=0:halt_on_error=1',UBSAN_OPTIONS='halt_on_error=1')
    with path.open('w') as output:
        process=subprocess.Popen([str(binary),'--trace',*(['--split'] if split else [])],cwd=ROOT,env=env,stdout=output,stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)

        def wait(predicate,label,timeout=20):
            end=time.monotonic()+timeout
            while time.monotonic()<end:
                assert process.poll() is None, path.read_text()[-6000:]
                current=states(path)
                if current and predicate(current[-1]): return current[-1]
                time.sleep(.04)
            raise AssertionError(label+'\n'+path.read_text()[-5000:])

        def settled(previous):
            return wait(lambda s:s['frame']>previous['frame']+2 and s['installed']==s['revision'] and s['completed_revision']==s['revision'],'settled latest revision')

        def capture(name):
            from PIL import Image
            file=BUILD/f'milestone-6-atelier-window-{suffix}-{name}.png'
            subprocess.run(['import','-window',str(x.owned),str(file)],check=True,timeout=10)
            image=Image.open(file).convert('RGB')
            assert len(image.getcolors(image.width*image.height) or [])>3
            return image.tobytes()

        try:
            end=time.monotonic()+15
            while not x.find(process.pid):
                assert process.poll() is None,path.read_text()[-5000:]
                assert time.monotonic()<end,'default Atelier window missing'
                time.sleep(.04)
            x.focus();x.move(292,210)
            initial=wait(lambda s:s['frame']>=4 and s['chunks']>0 and s['uploads']==4*s['chunks'] and s['installed']==0 and s['completed_revision']==0,'actual Atelier initial presentation')
            assert initial['quads']==10304
            assert 0 < initial['shadow_quads'] < initial['quads']
            intact=capture('intact')
            x.button(1,1);x.button(1,0)
            carved=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==1 and s['uploads']>initial['uploads'],'actual Atelier click edit'))
            assert (carved['uploads']-initial['uploads'])%4==0
            cut=capture('carved');assert cut!=intact
            assert carved['quads']!=initial['quads']
            x.tap(ord('r'))
            reset=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==2 and s['uploads']>carved['uploads'],'selected original Atelier reset'))
            assert reset['quads']==initial['quads']
            assert capture('reset')==intact
            x.tap(32)
            space=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==3 and s['uploads']>reset['uploads'],'Space must cut current Atelier hover'))
            assert capture('space')==cut
            assert space['quads']==carved['quads']
            assert space['uploads']-reset['uploads']==carved['uploads']-initial['uploads']
            x.tap(ord('r')); restored=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==4,'second reset'))
            x.key(ord('w'),1);time.sleep(.12);x.key(ord('w'),0)
            flown=settled(wait(lambda s:s['camera']!=restored['camera'],'Atelier flight'))
            assert flown['uploads']==restored['uploads']
            x.move(320,240);x.button(3,1)
            wait(lambda s:s['captured']==1,'Atelier pointer capture')
            os.kill(process.pid,signal.SIGSTOP)
            try:x.moves([(332,243),(342,249)])
            finally:os.kill(process.pid,signal.SIGCONT)
            looked=wait(lambda s:s['camera']!=flown['camera'],'Atelier captured look')
            x.button(3,0);settled(wait(lambda s:s['captured']==0,'Atelier capture release'))
            capture('flight-look')
            previous=looked
            for w,h in [(800,450),(450,900),(640,480)]:
                x.resize(w,h)
                previous=wait(lambda s:s['width']==w and s['height']==h and s['generation']>previous['generation'] and s['frame']>previous['frame']+2,'Atelier target recreation')
                assert previous['uploads']==restored['uploads'],'Resize uploaded geometry'
                capture(f'{w}x{h}')
            x.map(False)
            asleep=wait(lambda s:s['mapped']==0,'Atelier suspension')
            time.sleep(.2)
            assert states(path)[-1]['frame']<=asleep['frame']+2
            x.map(True);remapped=wait(lambda s:s['mapped']==1 and s['frame']>asleep['frame']+2,'Atelier remap')
            capture('remapped')
            x.close();process.wait(timeout=15)
            result=path.read_text()
            assert process.returncode==0,result[-8000:]
            assert 'Native interactive shutdown rows=0' in result
            assert not any(marker in result for marker in ('Validation Error','SYNC-HAZARD','AddressSanitizer','runtime error:'))
            queues=re.search(r'Queues (\d+) (\d+)',result)
            assert queues and ((queues[1]!=queues[2]) if split else (queues[1]==queues[2]))
            values=states(path)
            steady=[s['rows'] for s in values if s['revision']==4 and s['completed_revision']==4 and s['frame']>restored['frame']+2]
            assert steady and max(steady)-min(steady)<=4,'Settled Atelier reset/resize resources grew'
            assert abs(restored['rows']-reset['rows'])<=4,'Repeated reset retained obsolete chunk generations'
            print(f'Actual default Atelier {suffix} edit/Space/reset/flight/capture/resize/suspend/remap/close passed')
        finally:
            if process.poll() is None:
                process.terminate()
                try:process.wait(timeout=5)
                except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:process.kill();process.wait()
            x.x.XCloseDisplay(x.d)


def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--binary',type=Path)
    parser.add_argument('--sanitize',action='store_true')
    parser.add_argument('--isolated-display',action='store_true')
    args=parser.parse_args()
    binary=args.binary.resolve() if args.binary else build_window(args.sanitize,compile_timeout=COMPILE_TIMEOUT)
    with isolated_display(args.isolated_display):
        for split in (False,True):run(binary,split)


if __name__=='__main__':main()

def states(log):
    result=[]
    for line in log.read_text().split('\n')[:-1]:
        if line.startswith('STATE '):
            value={k: int(v) if v.isdigit() else v for k,v in re.findall(r'(\w+)=([^ ]+)',line)}
            if isinstance(value.get('camera'),str) and value['camera'].count(',')==4:
                result.append(value)
    return result

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import os
from pathlib import Path
import re
import signal
import subprocess
import time

from check_window import X11, states, isolated_display, build_window, BUILD, ROOT

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=1800


def run(binary, split):
    suffix='split' if split else 'shared'
    path=BUILD/f'milestone-6-atelier-window-{suffix}.log'
    x=X11()
    env=dict(os.environ,VK_INSTANCE_LAYERS='VK_LAYER_KHRONOS_validation',VK_LAYER_VALIDATE_SYNC='1',
             ASAN_OPTIONS='detect_leaks=0:halt_on_error=1',UBSAN_OPTIONS='halt_on_error=1')
    with path.open('w') as output:
        process=subprocess.Popen([str(binary),'--trace',*(['--split'] if split else [])],cwd=ROOT,env=env,stdout=output,stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)

        def wait(predicate,label,timeout=20):
            end=time.monotonic()+timeout
            while time.monotonic()<end:
                assert process.poll() is None, path.read_text()[-6000:]
                current=states(path)
                if current and predicate(current[-1]): return current[-1]
                time.sleep(.04)
            raise AssertionError(label+'\n'+path.read_text()[-5000:])

        def settled(previous):
            return wait(lambda s:s['frame']>previous['frame']+2 and s['installed']==s['revision'],'settled latest revision')

        def capture(name):
            from PIL import Image
            file=BUILD/f'milestone-6-atelier-window-{suffix}-{name}.png'
            subprocess.run(['import','-window',str(x.owned),str(file)],check=True,timeout=10)
            image=Image.open(file).convert('RGB')
            assert len(image.getcolors(image.width*image.height) or [])>3
            return image.tobytes()

        try:
            end=time.monotonic()+15
            while not x.find(process.pid):
                assert process.poll() is None,path.read_text()[-5000:]
                assert time.monotonic()<end,'default Atelier window missing'
                time.sleep(.04)
            x.focus();x.move(292,210)
            initial=wait(lambda s:s['frame']>=4 and s['uploads']==2 and s['installed']==0,'actual Atelier initial presentation')
            intact=capture('intact')
            x.button(1,1);x.button(1,0)
            carved=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==1 and s['uploads']==4,'actual Atelier click edit'))
            cut=capture('carved');assert cut!=intact
            assert carved['quads']!=initial['quads']
            x.tap(ord('r'))
            reset=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==2 and s['uploads']==6,'selected original Atelier reset'))
            assert reset['quads']==initial['quads']
            assert capture('reset')==intact
            x.tap(32)
            space=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==3 and s['uploads']==8,'Space must cut current Atelier hover'))
            assert capture('space')==cut
            assert space['quads']==carved['quads']
            x.tap(ord('r')); restored=settled(wait(lambda s:s['revision']==4,'second reset'))
            x.key(ord('w'),1);time.sleep(.12);x.key(ord('w'),0)
            flown=settled(wait(lambda s:s['camera']!=restored['camera'],'Atelier flight'))
            assert flown['uploads']==restored['uploads']
            x.move(320,240);x.button(3,1)
            wait(lambda s:s['captured']==1,'Atelier pointer capture')
            os.kill(process.pid,signal.SIGSTOP)
            try:x.moves([(332,243),(342,249)])
            finally:os.kill(process.pid,signal.SIGCONT)
            looked=wait(lambda s:s['camera']!=flown['camera'],'Atelier captured look')
            x.button(3,0);settled(wait(lambda s:s['captured']==0,'Atelier capture release'))
            capture('flight-look')
            previous=looked
            for w,h in [(800,450),(450,900),(640,480)]:
                x.resize(w,h)
                previous=wait(lambda s:s['width']==w and s['height']==h and s['generation']>previous['generation'] and s['frame']>previous['frame']+2,'Atelier target recreation')
                assert previous['uploads']==restored['uploads'],'Resize uploaded geometry'
                capture(f'{w}x{h}')
            x.map(False)
            asleep=wait(lambda s:s['mapped']==0,'Atelier suspension')
            time.sleep(.2)
            assert states(path)[-1]['frame']<=asleep['frame']+1
            x.map(True);remapped=wait(lambda s:s['mapped']==1 and s['frame']>asleep['frame']+2,'Atelier remap')
            capture('remapped')
            x.close();process.wait(timeout=15)
            result=path.read_text()
            assert process.returncode==0,result[-8000:]
            assert 'Native interactive shutdown rows=0' in result
            assert not any(marker in result for marker in ('Validation Error','SYNC-HAZARD','AddressSanitizer','runtime error:'))
            queues=re.search(r'Queues (\d+) (\d+)',result)
            assert queues and ((queues[1]!=queues[2]) if split else (queues[1]==queues[2]))
            values=states(path)
            steady=[s['rows'] for s in values if s['generation']>=1 and s['uploads']>=2]
            assert max(steady)-min(steady)<=8,'Atelier edit/resize resources grew'
            print(f'Actual default Atelier {suffix} edit/Space/reset/flight/capture/resize/suspend/remap/close passed')
        finally:
            if process.poll() is None:
                process.terminate()
                try:process.wait(timeout=5)
                except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:process.kill();process.wait()
            x.x.XCloseDisplay(x.d)


def main():
    parser=argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--binary',type=Path)
    parser.add_argument('--sanitize',action='store_true')
    parser.add_argument('--isolated-display',action='store_true')
    args=parser.parse_args()
    binary=args.binary.resolve() if args.binary else build_window(args.sanitize,compile_timeout=COMPILE_TIMEOUT)
    with isolated_display(args.isolated_display):
        for split in (False,True):run(binary,split)


if __name__=='__main__':main()

description: Cut AI tells from any writing.

# Unslop

Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.

## Patterns to detect and fix

Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

### Content

3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

name: technical-writing
description: "Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Technical writing

The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read. Four layers get you there, one question each: what kind of document is this, how do sentences address the reader, how much does each sentence carry, and can any sentence be read two ways. Apply all four.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** The rules serve the reader. A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill.

## Vary the rhythm

The layers decide what a document says and how much each sentence carries. A doc can obey all of them and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones that take their time carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

One document, one mode. Two questions pick it: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?

- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.

Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence.

**Tutorial: learning by doing.** You are the teacher. The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Teaching pauses break the lesson. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."

**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence. Skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".

**Reference: facts for lookup.** Describe. Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure. State facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible, so it stays true.

**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.

Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.

## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)

- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete." The reader skips what does not apply.
- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial.

## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)

- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can. They take too many grammatical jobs and breed misreadings.

## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)

- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
- Keep the small words that show structure. "Ensure that the switch is off" keeps "that" because it makes the sentence parse one way. Never trade clarity for word count.
- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread: "the client and the host", not "the client and host", when they are two things.
- Say which parts "and" or "or" joins when a sentence can group two ways. "Both...and", "either...or", and "if...then" are free disambiguators.
- Use periods, not semicolons. Replace an em dash with a new sentence.
- Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit or its own sentence. Never form plurals with "(s)".
- No slashes: write "a, b, or both" instead of "a/b" or "and/or".
- Call each thing by one name, everywhere. A doc that says "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" for one thing teaches three things. Rewording an unchanged sentence between edits costs the same way. Don't churn what didn't change.
- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors. A non-native reader, a translator, and an agent all parse plain constructions best.

## Voice and repo specifics

- Apply the **unslop** skill to every doc this skill touches. That skill owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, formatting tells.
- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them. A PR body is a briefing that a reviewer can read in under a minute. Do not paste swarm logs, SHA lists, or metric tables. Link them.
- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths and real symbols. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it.

## Worked example

Before:

> Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails.

After:

> `budget.mjs` reads the committed budget from `budget.json` and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run `budget.mjs --write` only to lower the budget.

5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

description: "Layered technical-writing standard: Diátaxis structure, Google developer style sentences, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Use for /technical-writing or when writing or reviewing docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, or commit messages."

# Technical writing

The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read. Four layers get you there, one question each: what kind of document is this, how do sentences address the reader, how much does each sentence carry, and can any sentence be read two ways. Apply all four.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** The rules serve the reader. A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Propose a new offender and its replacement as an addition to `unslop`'s abstract-metaphor rule in your reply, with the diff. Don't edit that skill.

## Vary the rhythm

The layers decide what a document says and how much each sentence carries. A doc can obey all of them and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones that take their time carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

One document, one mode. Two questions pick it: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?

- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.

Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence.

**Tutorial: learning by doing.** You are the teacher. The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Teaching pauses break the lesson. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."

**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence. Skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".

**Reference: facts for lookup.** Describe. Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure. State facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible, so it stays true.

**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.

Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.

## Write sentences to the reader (Google developer style)

- Talk to the reader as "you", in the present tense. "Will" only for things that genuinely happen later.
- Say who does what: "the compiler checks", not "is checked". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or beside the point.
- Write instructions as commands: "Click Submit." State facts plainly. Never "should be done".
- Put the condition before the instruction: "To delete the document, click Delete." The reader skips what does not apply.
- Put the common case first. Exceptions after.
- Sound like a knowledgeable friend. No buzzwords, no figurative language, no "please" in instructions, and never "simply", "easy", or "quickly" in a procedure. If it were simple, the reader would not be here.
- Don't pre-announce ("we will soon support...") and don't start consecutive sentences with the same phrase.
- Link with words that say where the link goes: the page title or a short description. Never "click here". Prefer a sentence of context on the page over a link off it.
- Headings carry the point, not just the topic ("Pick the mode first", not "Modes"). Sentence case. A task heading is a bare verb phrase ("Create an instance"). A concept heading is a noun phrase. One h1 per page, no skipped levels.
- Numbered lists for sequences, bullets for everything else. Introduce a list with a complete sentence. Keep items parallel.
- Code goes in code font. UI elements go in bold. Use serial commas. Drop "etc." and say up front that a list is partial.

## Make statements load one at a time (STE rules)

- One instruction per sentence. One thought per sentence everywhere else.
- Split instructions longer than about 20 words and other sentences longer than about 25.
- Put the warning or condition before the step it guards: "If hot oil touches your skin, injuries can occur."
- Keep "the" and "a": "Remove backup file" reads two ways. "Remove the backup file" reads one.
- Give each word one meaning and one job, then keep it. If "check" means inspect, don't also use it for restrain.
- Pick one word per action and stick to it: "start", not "start" here and "initiate" there.
- Write procedures as direct commands, never as narration and never in the passive: "Install the component", not "the component must be installed".
- Avoid "-ing" words where you can. They take too many grammatical jobs and breed misreadings.

## Leave no sentence open to two readings (Global English)

- Keep words like "only" and "not" next to the word they change: "only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.
- Break up long noun strings: "the proto import budget check script" becomes "the script that checks the proto-import budget".
- Make every "it", "they", and "this" point at one obvious thing. Repeat the noun when in doubt. Never use "this" or "which" to point at a whole clause.
- Don't drop verbs: "Phase 1 moves the converters and Phase 2 the runtime" leaves Phase 2 without one. Give it one.
- Keep the small words that show structure. "Ensure that the switch is off" keeps "that" because it makes the sentence parse one way. Never trade clarity for word count.
- Repeat the article in a series when it prevents a misread: "the client and the host", not "the client and host", when they are two things.
- Say which parts "and" or "or" joins when a sentence can group two ways. "Both...and", "either...or", and "if...then" are free disambiguators.
- Use periods, not semicolons. Replace an em dash with a new sentence.
- Make text in parentheses a full grammatical unit or its own sentence. Never form plurals with "(s)".
- No slashes: write "a, b, or both" instead of "a/b" or "and/or".
- Call each thing by one name, everywhere. A doc that says "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" for one thing teaches three things. Rewording an unchanged sentence between edits costs the same way. Don't churn what didn't change.
- Skip idioms, colloquialisms, Latin abbreviations, and metaphors. A non-native reader, a translator, and an agent all parse plain constructions best.

## Voice and repo specifics

- Apply the **unslop** skill to every doc this skill touches. That skill owns the slop-pattern catalog: AI vocabulary, filler, hedging, formatting tells.
- PR descriptions and commit messages are writing too. Every layer except Diátaxis applies to them. A PR body is a briefing that a reviewer can read in under a minute. Do not paste swarm logs, SHA lists, or metric tables. Link them.
- Product UI strings are not documentation. Use your product's copy guidelines for those.
- Indent code snippets with tabs. Write real paths and real symbols. Make every count or tree claim true at the commit that lands it, and include the command that regenerates it.

## Worked example

Before:

> Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails.

After:

> `budget.mjs` reads the committed budget from `budget.json` and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run `budget.mjs --write` only to lower the budget.
